triples.source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: ‘Your wife will practice prostitution in the city, your sons and daughters will fall by a sword, and your land will be measured out with a cord. You will die in an unclean land, and Israel will be led captive away from its land.’”

target_units.text: Because thus says the Lord: Behold, I am giving you to migration with all your friends. They will fall by their enemies’ sword, and your eyes will see. I will give you and all Judah into the hands of Babylon’s king, and they will deport them and cut them down with swords.
And I will give all this city’s strength, all its labors, and all the treasures of Judah’s king into his enemies’ hands, and they will bring them to Babylon.
And you and all who dwell in your house will go into captivity. In Babylon you will die and there be buried—you and all your friends to whom you prophesied false things.

triples.relationship: a priest opposing a prophet is warned of sword, captivity and death abroad
triples.rationale: Amos's response to Amaziah announces deaths by sword, captivity and his death in an unclean land. Jeremiah's response to Pashhur likewise announces sword deaths among his associates and captivity ending in his death in Babylon. The surrounding accounts identify each opponent as a priest who acts against the prophet.

triples.source_text: He said, “What do you see, Amos?” I said, “A fowler’s vessel.” The Lord said to me, “The end has arrived upon My people Israel. I will certainly no longer pass them by.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, say, ‘Thus says the Lord to the land of Israel: An end has come; the end has come upon the four wings of the land.
The end has come
upon you, inhabitant of the land. The time has come; the day has drawn near, neither with tumult nor with birth pangs.

triples.relationship: the announced arrival of an end upon Israel
triples.rationale: Amos's vision is explained by the declaration that the end has arrived upon the Lord's people Israel. Ezekiel likewise addresses Israel's land with the repeated declaration that an end has come upon it and its inhabitants. Both declare the arrival of an end in a judgment oracle.

triples.source_text: Hear these things now, you who wear out the needy until morning and oppress the poor out of the land,

target_units.text: Do not use force against the needy, for he is poor, and do not dishonor the weak at the gates;
for the Lord will judge his case, and you will preserve your own life unplundered.

triples.relationship: oppression of the needy opposed to the prohibition of force
triples.rationale: Amos addresses those who wear out the needy and oppress the poor out of the land. Proverbs explicitly forbids force against the needy and dishonoring the weak, adding that the Lord will judge the poor person's case.

triples.source_text: saying, “When will the month pass, so we may trade, and the sabbaths, so we may open storehouses, making the measure small and the weights great and making an unjust balance,

target_units.text: You shall not have in your pouch differing weights, a great and a small.
You shall not have in your house differing measures, a great and a small.
You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.
For everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination unto the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: unjust commercial measurements opposed to the legal standard
triples.rationale: Amos reports traders planning a small measure, great weights and an unjust balance. Deuteronomy forbids differing weights and measures, requires true and just ones, and condemns those who practice that injustice.

triples.source_text: to acquire the poor with silver and a lowly person in exchange for sandals? And we will trade from every kind of produce.”

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sold a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals,

triples.relationship: same-book exchange of vulnerable people for silver and sandals
triples.rationale: Amos 8 reports an intention to acquire poor people for silver and a lowly person for sandals. Amos 2 condemns selling a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals. The repeated prices connect buying and selling within the book's accusations of exploitation.

triples.source_text: The Lord swears by Jacob’s arrogance: “He will never forget all your works.”

target_units.text: so that they sing together as people singing together with their heart. I remembered all their evils; now their schemes have surrounded them; they have come before My face.

triples.rationale: Following the charges of oppression and unjust trade, the oath in Amos declares that the people's works will never be forgotten. Hosea likewise speaks of all their evils remembered and their schemes coming before the Lord's face. Amos's oath by Jacob's arrogance is preserved without changing its stated object.

triples.source_text: Will the earth not be disturbed over these things, and everyone dwelling in it mourn? A consummation will rise like a river and descend like Egypt’s river.

target_units.text: The Lord, Lord God Almighty, touches the earth and shakes it; all who dwell in it will mourn. Its consummation will rise like a river and descend like Egypt’s river.

triples.relationship: same-book recurrence of earth's disturbance and Egypt's river
triples.rationale: Both passages join the disturbed or shaken earth with its inhabitants mourning and a consummation rising like a river and descending like Egypt's river. Amos 9 explicitly introduces the Lord touching the earth within this repeated description.

triples.source_text: “On that day,” says the Lord God, “the sun will set at midday, and the light will grow dark upon the earth in daytime.

target_units.text: She who bore seven was emptied; her soul grew faint. Her sun set while the day was still at its middle; she was ashamed and reproached. Their remnants I will give to the sword before their enemies.

triples.relationship: sunset during the middle of the day as judgment imagery
triples.rationale: Amos announces the sun setting at midday and daylight growing dark upon the earth. Jeremiah likewise describes the sun of the woman who bore seven setting while the day is still at its middle, beside shame and threatened sword deaths. Both use the unexpected midday sunset in a judgment setting.

triples.source_text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

target_units.text: Daughter of My people, gird yourself with sackcloth; sprinkle yourself with ashes. Make mourning for yourself for a beloved one, a pitiful lament, because misery will suddenly come upon you.

triples.relationship: sackcloth and mourning for a beloved one
triples.rationale: Amos joins sackcloth with lamentation and mourning for a beloved one. Jeremiah likewise tells the daughter of the people to wear sackcloth and make a pitiful lament for a beloved one because misery is coming.

triples.source_text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

target_units.text: and they will gird on sackcloth; amazement will cover them, shame will be upon every face among them, and baldness upon every head.

triples.relationship: shared public mourning signs of sackcloth and baldness
triples.rationale: Amos announces sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head. Ezekiel likewise describes people girding on sackcloth, shame upon every face and baldness upon every head. Both extend these mourning signs across the judged population.

triples.source_text: Look, days are coming,” says the Lord, “when I will send famine upon the earth: not famine for bread or thirst for water, but famine for hearing the Lord’s word.

target_units.text: And He afflicted you, and made you hunger, and fed you with manna, which your fathers did not know, that He might declare unto you that man shall not live by bread alone, but man shall live by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.

triples.relationship: bread and the Lord's word distinguished as human necessities
triples.rationale: Amos announces a famine for hearing the Lord's word rather than for bread or water. Deuteronomy recounts hunger and manna to explain that a person lives by every word from God's mouth and not by bread alone. Both distinguish dependence on God's word from physical bread.

triples.source_text: Waters will be shaken as far as the sea, and from north to east they will run about seeking the Lord’s word, but certainly will not find it.

target_units.text: Saul saw the foreigners’ camp and was afraid, and his heart was greatly astounded.
Saul inquired through the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him by dreams, by clear signs, or by prophets.

triples.relationship: seeking divine communication without receiving an answer
triples.rationale: Amos describes people running about seeking the Lord's word but not finding it. Samuel's account describes Saul inquiring through the Lord while receiving no answer through dreams, clear signs or prophets. Both describe an unsuccessful search for divine communication, in different settings.

triples.source_text: On that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will faint from thirst,

target_units.text: The nursing child’s tongue clung to its throat with thirst. Infants asked for bread; there is no one to break it for them.

triples.relationship: young people pictured with thirst in calamity
triples.rationale: Amos foretells young women and men fainting from thirst. Lamentations portrays a nursing child's tongue clinging to its throat with thirst, alongside infants asking for bread. Both use images of bodily thirst among the young, while the age groups and exact effects differ.

triples.source_text: those who swear by Samaria’s propitiation and say, ‘Your god lives, Dan!’ and ‘Your god lives, Beersheba!’ They will fall and certainly never rise again.”

target_units.text: The king took counsel, went, and made two golden heifers. He said to the people, “Let your going up to Jerusalem be enough. Behold, your gods, Israel, who brought you up from Egypt!”
He placed one in Bethel and put the other in Dan.
This matter became a sin. The people went before the one as far as Dan.

triples.relationship: the condemned cult of Dan and its golden heifer
triples.rationale: Amos condemns people who declare that Dan's god lives. Kings records one of the two golden heifers being placed in Dan and calls the resulting practice a sin. The connection concerns Dan's cult; Amos's separate wording about Samaria's propitiation and Beersheba remains unchanged.
